<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
An \emph{abstract simplicial complex} $K$ on a vertex set $V(K)$ is a collection of finite nonempty subsets of $V(K)$ such that, whenever $\sigma\in K$ and $\varnothing\neq\tau\subseteq\sigma$, we have $\tau\in K$. The elements of $K$ are called \emph{simplices}, and the dimension of a simplex $\sigma$ is defined by $$ \dim \sigma = |\sigma|-1. $$ A simplex is \emph{maximal} if it is not properly contained in any other simplex of $K$. The dimension of $K$ is $$\dim K=\max\{\dim\sigma:\sigma\in K\}.$$
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $K$ be a simplicial complex and let $u,v\in V(K)$ with $u\neq v$.
The vertex $v$ is said to be \emph{dominated} by $u$ if every maximal
simplex of $K$ containing $v$ also contains $u$. Equivalently, $$\operatorname{lk}_K(v)\subseteq \operatorname{st}_K(u).$$
In this case, the deletion of $v$, together with all simplices containing
it, is called an \emph{elementary strong collapse}. A finite sequence of
elementary strong collapses is called a \emph{strong collapse}. The complex
$K$ is \emph{strongly collapsible} if it strongly collapses to a single
vertex.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
~\cite{FMV2015}
The \emph{simplicial geometric category} of a finite
simplicial complex $K$, denoted by $\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(K)$, is the least integer $m\geq0$ such that $$K=C_0\cup C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_m,$$
where each $C_i$ is strongly collapsible. Notice that strongly collapsible subcomplexes must be connected.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
A graph is a \emph{forest} if it contains no cycles. Equivalently, each connected component of a forest is a tree.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A cactus graph is a connected graph in which every edge belongs to
at most one cycle. Equivalently, any two distinct cycles have at most one vertex in common.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and let $S\subseteq V$. The subgraph of $G$ induced by $S$, denoted by $G[S]$, is the graph with vertex set $S$ and edge set $$E(G[S])=\{uv\in E\mid u,v\in S\}.$$ In other words, $G[S]$ contains all edges of $G$ whose endpoints both belong to $S$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let $G$ be a graph. If $E(G)\neq\varnothing$, let $k$ be the minimum number of forests whose edge sets partition $E(G)$. The
(reduced) \emph{arboricity} of $G$ is defined by $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)=k-1.$
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:nw} For every graph $G$ containing at least one edge, $$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)=\max\left\{0, \,\max_{\substack{H\subseteq G\\|V(H)|\geq2}}\left\lceil\frac{|E(H)|}{|V(H)|-1}\right\rceil-1\right\}.$$
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
Let $K$ and $L$ be graphs sharing exactly one vertex $v$ and otherwise
disjoint. Their \emph{wedges}, denoted by $K\vee_vL$, is their union after
the two chosen copies of $v$ have been identified.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Let $G_1=(V_1,E_1)$ and $G_2=(V_2,E_2)$ have disjoint vertex sets.
The \emph{join} $G_1\mathbin{*} G_2$ is the graph with
$$E(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)=E_1\cup E_2\cup\{uv:u\in V_1,\ v\in V_2\}.$$
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:mono}
If $H\subseteq G$, then $$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(H)\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G).$$
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Restrict any forest decomposition of $G$ to $H$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:edgebound}
Let $G$ be a graph with $|V(G)|=n\geq 1$. If $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\leq t$, where $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}$ denotes the reduced arboricity, then $$|E(G)|\leq (t+1)(n-1).$$
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\leq t$, the edge set of $G$ can be partitioned into at most $t+1$ forests. Each forest on $n$ vertices has at most $n-1$ edges. Therefore, $$|E(G)|\leq (t+1)(n-1).$$
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:bipdensity}
For positive integers $s,t$, define $$g(s,t)=\frac{st}{s+t-1}.$$ Then $g$ is nondecreasing in each variable.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Fix $t\geq1$. For every $s\geq1$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
g(s+1,t)-g(s,t)
&=
\frac{(s+1)t}{s+t}
-
\frac{st}{s+t-1}= \\
&=
\frac{t(t-1)}{(s+t)(s+t-1)}
\geq0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $g(s,t)$ is nondecreasing in $s$. By symmetry, it is also
nondecreasing in $t$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:kmn}
For positive integers $m,n$, $$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_{m,n})=\left\lceil\frac{mn}{m+n-1}\right\rceil-1.$$
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Taking the whole vertex set of $K_{m,n}$ in
Theorem~\ref{thm:nw} gives $$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_{m,n})\geq\left\lceil
\frac{|E(K_{m,n})|}{|V(K_{m,n})|-1}\right\rceil-1=\left\lceil\frac{mn}{m+n-1}\right\rceil-1.$$

For the reverse inequality, let $S\subseteq V(K_{m,n})$ with
$|S|\geq2$. Suppose that $S$ contains $s$ vertices from the first
part and $t$ vertices from the second part. Then $|E(K_{m,n}[S])|=st$ and $|S|-1=s+t-1.$ If $s=0$ or $t=0$, then $K_{m,n}[S]$ has no edges, and hence$$\frac{|E(K_{m,n}[S])|}{|S|-1}=0.$$
If $s,t\geq1$, then $s\leq m$ and $t\leq n$, so Lemma~\ref{lem:bipdensity} gives $$ \frac{|E(K_{m,n}[S])|}{|S|-1}=\frac{st}{s+t-1}\leq\frac{mn}{m+n-1}.$$
Therefore, for every $S\subseteq V(K_{m,n})$ with $|S|\geq2$,
$$\left\lceil\frac{|E(K_{m,n}[S])|}{|S|-1}\right\rceil\leq \left\lceil\frac{mn}{m+n-1}\right\rceil.$$Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:nw}, we obtain$$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_{m,n})\leq\left\lceil\frac{mn}{m+n-1}\right\rceil-1.$$
Combining the two inequalities proves the result.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:complete}
For every $n\geq2$, $$ \ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_n)=\left\lceil\frac{n}{2}\right\rceil-1. $$
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
An induced copy of $K_s$ has density $$ \frac{\binom{s}{2}}{s-1}=\frac{s}{2},$$
which is maximized at $s=n$. We apply Theorem~\ref{thm:nw} to get the statement of Corollary \ref{cor:complete}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:graph-gscat}
Let $G$ be a connected graph containing at least one edge. Then $$ \ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G). $$
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Briefly, a strongly collapsible one-dimensional complex is a tree. A decomposition of $G$ into $a=\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)+1$ forests can be enlarged, inside the connected graph $G$, to a cover by $a$ trees;
hence $\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G)\leq a-1=\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)$. Conversely, from a cover by $m+1$ trees, assign
each edge to one tree containing it. The assigned edge sets are forests and
partition $E(G)$, so $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\leq m$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:wedge} Let $G=K\vee_v L$ be the wedges of $K$ and $L$ at $v$. Then $$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)=\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K),\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(L)\}.$$
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
\emph{Lower bound.} Since $K,L\subseteq G$ as subgraphs, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\ge\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K)$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\ge\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(L)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}. Hence, we obtain that $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\ge\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K),\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(L)\}.$

\emph{Upper bound.} Let $H\subseteq G$, $|V(H)|\ge 2$, attain the maximum in Theorem~\ref{thm:nw} for $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)$, and set $H_K:=H\cap K$, $H_L:=H\cap L$. We first consider the case when $H$ is contained entirely in one of the two graphs. If $H\subseteq K$ (or $H\subseteq L$), then trivially inequalities hold: $\lceil|E(H)|/(|V(H)|-1)\rceil-1\le\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K)\le\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K),\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(L)\}$.

It remains to consider the case when $H$ meets both $K\setminus\{v\}$ and $L\setminus\{v\}$. Since $v$ is the only vertex joining $K$ and $L$ in $G$, any path in $H$ from $K\setminus\{v\}$ to $L\setminus\{v\}$ must pass through $v$. Therefore, $v\in V(H)$. Moreover, since $E(K)\cap E(L)=\emptyset$, the edges of $H$ split into the edges lying in $H_K$ and those lying in $H_L$. Consequently, $$|E(H)|=|E(H_K)|+|E(H_L)|,\qquad |V(H)|=|V(H_K)|+|V(H_L)|-1,$$
where the second identity follows from the fact that $v$ is the only shared vertex of $H_K$ and $H_L$.

Now, writing $p=|E(H_K)|$, $q=|E(H_L)|$, $r=|V(H_K)|-1$, and $s=|V(H_L)|-1$, we have $|E(H)|=p+q$ and $|V(H)|-1=r+s$. If $r=0$, then $p=0$ as well, and therefore $(p+q)/(r+s)=q/s$. The case $s=0$ is symmetric. Otherwise, when both $r$ and $s$ are positive, the mediant inequality gives $$ \frac{|E(H)|}{|V(H)|-1}=\frac{p+q}{r+s}\le\max\left\{\frac{p}{r},\frac{q}{s}\right\}=$$ $$=\max\left(\frac{|E(H_K)|}{|V(H_K)|-1},\frac{|E(H_L)|}{|V(H_L)|-1}\right)\le\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K)+1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(L)+1\}.$$

Thus, in either case, the density of $H$ does not exceed $\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K)+1,\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(L)+1\}$. Since $\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K),\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(L)\}\in\mathbb Z$, taking ceilings and subtracting one gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\le\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K),\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(L)\}$.
Combining both bounds proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:iterated-wedge}
For a finite iterated wedges, $$ \ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}\left(\bigvee_{i=1}^{m}G_i\right) =\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_i)\}. $$
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:iterated-wedge-gscat}
Let $G_1,\ldots,G_m$ be connected graphs containing at least one edge. Then $$\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}\left(\bigvee_{i=1}^{m}G_i\right)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G_i)\}.$$
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
This follows immediately from Corollary~\ref{cor:iterated-wedge} and Theorem~\ref{thm:graph-gscat}, since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)$ for every connected graph containing at least one edge.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:bouquet}
Let $B=C_{n_1}\vee C_{n_2}\vee\cdots\vee C_{n_r},$ $n_i\geq3$ be a bouquet of cycles (see Figure ~\ref{fig:bouquet}). For every cycle $C_n$ gives
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(C_n)=1$. Then Corollary~\ref{cor:iterated-wedge} gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(B)=1.$ Since $B$ is connected, Corollary~\ref{cor:iterated-wedge-gscat} also gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(B)=1$. Alternatively, we can cover B with two explicits trees (see Figure ~\ref{fig:bouquet}).
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Let G be a Cactus graph (see Figure ~\ref{fig:cactus} (a),(b)). Recall that every connected cactus graph is obtained by successively attaching blocks
that are either single edges or cycles at cut vertices. Since
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_2)=0$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(C_n)=1$, Corollary~\ref{cor:iterated-wedge} implies
$$
\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)=
\begin{cases}
0, & \text{if $G$ is a tree},\\
1, & \text{if $G$ contains a cycle}.
\end{cases}
$$
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:dense-wedge}
Consider the following graph $G=K_4 \vee K_5$ (see Figure ~\ref{fig:dense-wedge}). By Corollary~\ref{cor:complete},
$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_5)=2$ and $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_4)=1$. Hence $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)=\max\{2,1\}=2$
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:join}
Let $G_i=(V_i,E_i)$ be graphs with $|V_i|=n_i\geq 1$, for $i=1,2$, and set $$B=\left\lceil\frac{n_1n_2}{n_1+n_2-1}\right\rceil-1.$$ Then $$\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1),\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2),B\}\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1)+\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2)+B+1.$$
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
\emph{Lower bound.}
The subgraph of $G_1\mathbin{*} G_2$ induced by $V_1$ is exactly $G_1$, since the join operation adds no new edges between vertices of $V_1$. Thus, $G_1\subseteq G_1\mathbin{*} G_2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:mono} gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1)\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)$. By the same argument, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2)\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)$. Moreover, if we retain only the edges joining vertices of $V_1$ to vertices of $V_2$, we obtain the complete bipartite graph $K_{n_1,n_2}$. Hence, $K_{n_1,n_2}\subseteq G_1\mathbin{*} G_2$. Therefore, by Lemma~\ref{lem:mono} and Corollary~\ref{cor:kmn}, $B=\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_{n_1,n_2})\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)$. Combining these three inequalities, we obtain $$\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)\geq\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1),\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2),B\}.$$

\emph{Upper bound.}
Let $S\subseteq V_1\cup V_2$ be a subset with $|S|\geq2$, and set $S_1=S\cap V_1$ and $S_2=S\cap V_2$. The edges of the induced subgraph$(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)[S]$ consist of the edges of $G_1[S_1]$, the edges of $G_2[S_2]$, and all edges joining a vertex of $S_1$ to a vertex of $S_2$. Consequently,
$$|E((G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)[S])|=|E(G_1[S_1])|+|E(G_2[S_2])|+|S_1|\cdot|S_2|.$$

\emph{The first two terms.}
If $S_1=\emptyset$, then $|E(G_1[S_1])|=0$. Otherwise, let $k=|S_1|\geq1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1[S_1])\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1)$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:edgebound} therefore gives $|E(G_1[S_1])|\leq(\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1)+1)(k-1)$. Similarly, $|E(G_2[S_2])|\leq(\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2)+1)(|S_2|-1)$.

\emph{The cross term.}
Write $s=|S_1|\leq n_1$ and $t=|S_2|\leq n_2$. If $s=0$ or $t=0$, then the cross term is equal to zero. Suppose now that $s,t\geq1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:bipdensity}, $$g(s,t)\leq g(n_1,t)\leq g(n_1,n_2)=\frac{n_1n_2}{n_1+n_2-1}\leq B+1.$$ Since $g(s,t)=st/(s+t-1)$ and $s+t=|S|$, it follows that
$$|S_1||S_2|=g(s,t)(s+t-1)\leq(B+1)(|S|-1).$$

\emph{Combining the estimates.}
Suppose first that both $S_1$ and $S_2$ are nonempty. Adding the three estimates above, we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
|E((G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)[S])|
&\leq(\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1)+1)(|S_1|-1)+(\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2)+1)(|S_2|-1)+ \\
&\qquad +(B+1)(|S|-1).\end{aligned}$$
Since$(|S_1|-1)+(|S_2|-1)=|S|-2$, this implies $$|E((G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)[S])|\leq\bigl(\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1)+\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2)+B+2\bigr)(|S|-1).$$
If one of $S_1$ or $S_2$ is empty, the same estimate follows directly from Lemma~\ref{lem:mono}. Therefore, Theorem~\ref{thm:nw} gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1)+\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2)+B+1$.
Combining the lower and upper bounds, we conclude that
$$\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1),\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2),B\}\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_1)+\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G_2)+B+1.$$
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:join-gscat}
Let $G_i=(V_i,E_i)$ be connected graphs containing at least one edge, with $|V_i|=n_i$, for $i=1,2$, and set
$ B=\left\lceil\frac{n_1n_2}{n_1+n_2-1}\right\rceil-1.$ Then $$\max\{\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G_1),\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G_2),B\}\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G_1\mathbin{*} G_2)\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G_1)+\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(G_2)+B+1.$$
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
This follows immediately from Theorems~\ref{thm:join}
and~\ref{thm:graph-gscat}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:independent-join}
Let $G=\overline K_m\mathbin{*}\overline K_n=K_{m,n}$, where $m,n\geq1$ (see Figure~\ref{fig:independent-join}). Since $E(\overline K_m)=E(\overline K_n)=\varnothing$, we have $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(\overline K_m)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(\overline K_n)=0$. Setting $B=\left\lceil\frac{mn}{m+n-1}\right\rceil-1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:join} gives $B\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_{m,n})\leq B$. Therefore, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_{m,n})=\left\lceil\frac{mn}{m+n-1}\right\rceil-1$. Since $K_{m,n}$ is connected, Corollary~\ref{cor:join-gscat} also gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(K_{m,n})=\left\lceil\frac{mn}{m+n-1}\right\rceil-1$.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{ex:fan}
Let $F_n=K_1\mathbin{*} P_n$, where $P_n$ is the path on $n\geq2$ vertices (see Figure~\ref{fig:fan}). Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_1)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(P_n)=0$ and $B=\left\lceil\frac{n}{n}\right\rceil-1=0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:join} gives $0\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(F_n)\leq1$. Moreover, $F_n$ contains a triangle formed by the cone vertex and any edge of $P_n$, so $F_n$ is not a forest. Therefore, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(F_n)=1$. Since $F_n$ is connected, Corollary~\ref{cor:join-gscat} also gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(F_n)=1$.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{ex:path-independent}
Let $G=P_4\mathbin{*}\overline K_3$ (see Figure~\ref{fig:path-independent}). Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(P_4)=\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(\overline K_3)=0$ and $B=\left\lceil\frac{4\cdot3}{4+3-1}\right\rceil-1=1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:join} gives $1\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\leq2$. Moreover, $G$ has seven vertices and $|E(G)|=|E(P_4)|+4\cdot3=3+12=15$. Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:nw} to the full vertex set gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(G)\geq\left\lceil\frac{15}{7-1}\right\rceil-1=2$. Therefore, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(P_4\mathbin{*}\overline K_3)=2$. Since $G$ is connected, Corollary~\ref{cor:join-gscat} also gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(P_4\mathbin{*}\overline K_3)=2$.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{ex:wheel}
Let $W_n=K_1\mathbin{*} C_{n-1}$, where $n\geq4$ (see Figure~\ref{fig:wheel}). Since $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(K_1)=0$, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(C_{n-1})=1$, and $B=\left\lceil\frac{n-1}{n-1}\right\rceil-1=0$, Theorem~\ref{thm:join} gives $1\leq\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(W_n)\leq2$. The upper bound can be sharpened directly. Label the rim vertices by $v_1,\ldots,v_{n-1}$ and the hub by $h$. One forest consists of the rim path $v_1v_2,v_2v_3,\ldots,v_{n-2}v_{n-1}$ together with the spoke $hv_1$, while the second forest consists of the remaining rim edge $v_{n-1}v_1$ and the spokes $hv_2,\ldots,hv_{n-1}$. These two spanning trees contain every edge of $W_n$, so $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(W_n)\leq1$. Therefore, $\ensuremath{\mathrm{arb}}(W_n)=1$. Since $W_n$ is connected, Corollary~\ref{cor:join-gscat} also gives $\ensuremath{\mathrm{gscat}}(W_n)=1$.
<!-- end example-7 -->
